title: Are You An Exercise Non-Responder?
description: Do you get the feeling that your workouts just aren’t working? You show up day after day, week after week, month after month. You put in the work. And yet, the results don’t match the effort. You start to wonder: Shouldn’t I be seeing more gains for my effort? Am I just unlucky? It feels almost conspiratorial to say out loud. And nobody wants to be a whiner. So, you keep going, and you keep quiet. But that phenomenon is real. It’s been recognized for years. In fact, the fitness world even has a name for it: “ non-responders ” or “ low-responders ” to exercise. The implication is that some unlucky people just don’t respond as well. And it’s usually chalked up to bad genetics. The good news is that when you actually dig into the data, the story is far more nuanced, and far more actionable! Today, we’re delving into a study that cracks open the mystery of exercise “non-responsiveness.” And the answer isn’t genetics. It’s something else entirely that is completely within your control. Premium subscribers get full access to my deep dives into cutting-edge metabolic research for less than $1/letter, 3 per week. You’ll always walk away with at least one new insight about metabolic health. In the rest of this letter for StayCurious Metabolism Premium members, we dive into: The real culprit behind exercise non-responsiveness A combination of animal and human data Actionable strategies you can use today to get more out of every workout. If you want to join a community of people who care deeply about metabolic health, and who aren’t satisfied with surface-level answers, now is as good a time as any! If you don’t think you’re getting value, cancel at any time.

title: Lp(a) Masterclass: What It Is and What to Do About It
description: *News note: The big news of the last few days was the negative result of the Lp(a) HORIZON trial, a large Phase 3 trial in which an Lp(a)-lowering drug failed to reduce cardiovascular events. The cardiology world is in a little bit of a free fall right now. Whether or not you’re aware of this trial, I’ll provide my commentary in a postscript at the end. All the teachings herein still apply. You just get a little extra nuance. When I was first diagnosed with elevated Lp(a), I was scared. I knew what the numbers meant. Statistically, my lifetime risk of a heart attack was dramatically higher—perhaps by as much as 230% . And because heart disease runs in my family, this wasn’t just an abstract statistic. I inherited high Lp(a) from my father, who almost died of a heart attack at just 44 years old. I had every reason to be frightened. I’m not anymore. What changed wasn’t my genetics. My Lp(a) is still high. What changed was my understanding. The Lp(a) Myth Over the past few years, Lp(a) has gone from obscurity to becoming the newest cardiovascular supervillain. Darth Vader. Thanos. Voldemort. Pick your franchise. And if you’re interested in heart health, you’ve almost certainly heard that elevated Lp(a) substantially increases cardiovascular risk. What you may also have heard is that “ it’s almost entirely genetic .” And “ there are no medications available shown to lower Lp(a) and reduce cardiovascular risk .” Those statements have truth to them. There’s also, “ so there’s nothing you can do about it .” That one? That one is dead wrong. While your Lp(a) level is largely determined by your genes, the amount Lp(a) increases your cardiovascular risk is not. Point blank.

title: GLP-1s Extend Lifespan in Mice. What About Humans?
description: A drug just made old mice live 12% longer. Not a drug you’ve never heard of, but one that about 15 million Americans are already injecting into their bodies every week: a GLP-1. Now, the moment anyone tells you something extends lifespan, your skepticism should switch on like a hunger neuron at the sight of pecan pie. And I want you to hold on to that skepticism for this entire letter. It’s good because longevity claims are notoriously difficult to prove in humans. That’s why we often lean on animal studies. But animal longevity results have a long, humbling history of failing to translate to people. So, do the results of this new paper, published in Nature , mean you’ll live 12% longer if you start a GLP-1? Probably not. But I also think dismissing this as “just a mouse study” would cause you to miss the deeper point. The story here isn’t about just lifespan. It’s about seeing past the tip of the metabolic iceberg, to the far more fascinating belly beneath. So, let’s break down these new data and what they mean for you. And, at the end, we have a special treat, a StayCurious consultation with a double board-certified physician who has counseled hundreds of patients on peptides and longevity. But that will be your dessert. Finish your food first… The Mice That Lived 12% Longer The first experiment was the headline-grabber. Old mice (20 months, which is about 70-years-old in human years) were given semaglutide, a GLP-1 receptor agonist for three months. Treatment reduced food intake by 24%, drove weight loss, and significantly increased lifespan, with median lifespan increasing from 742 days in the control group to 834 days in the semaglutide group (12% increase in median lifespan).
